inputs.need:
I direct the simulation centre for a health authority with four hospitals, and I lead the education programme for their rapid response teams: a critical care nurse, a respiratory therapist and a physician on call for deteriorating ward patients. Each hospital runs its own training, mostly an annual lecture and an online module, and last year's case reviews found delays in recognising the need to escalate, poor role clarity when the team arrived, and handover problems when patients moved to intensive care. We want to introduce in-situ simulation: short, unannounced scenarios run on the wards with the real team every month, each followed by a structured debrief.

I would like to evaluate this as a multi-site mixed methods study across the four hospitals, introducing the programme one hospital at a time over a year. The quantitative strand would measure what happens in real rapid response calls: time from the call to the first critical intervention, unplanned intensive care admission after a call, and death within 24 hours, with team performance in the simulations as a secondary measure. The qualitative strand would explore how teams, ward nurses and families experience the calls and the simulations, through interviews and observation of debriefs. I need help with the design, the sample size given only four hospitals, measures that are not just checklist scores, and the ethics of unannounced simulations on working wards. Each hospital's education lead has agreed to take part, and we have a small grant.
inputs.constraints: A grant of 48,000 for 18 months; simulation faculty time is limited to 8 hours a month per hospital; unannounced simulations must never delay real patient care and must stop immediately if a real call occurs on the ward.
localFacts: The four hospitals' rapid response teams attended 2,860 calls last year, between 480 and 1,020 per hospital.
Education leads at all four hospitals signed letters of participation between 2026-08-20 and 2026-09-05.
The simulation education grant of 48,000 was awarded on 2026-07-30 (grant SEF-2026-14).
The health authority research ethics board is the board of record for multi-site studies; no application has been submitted yet.

records.title: In-situ simulation for rapid response teams and time to first critical intervention: a before-after study in one hospital
records.authors: Lindqvist-Oduya S, Marchetti-Brandt K, Achebe-Nakamura P
records.abstract: One hospital introduced monthly unannounced in-situ simulations for its rapid response team, each followed by a structured debrief. We compared 12 months of real calls before and after the change. The median time from call to first critical intervention fell from 11.2 to 8.4 minutes. Unplanned intensive care admission after a call did not change. The study had no control group, a new early warning score was introduced during the after period, and the team members changed over the two years, so the fall cannot be attributed to simulation alone.

records.title: A stepped-wedge evaluation of in-situ simulation for medical emergency teams across five hospitals
records.authors: Ferreira-Holm D, Okafor-Lindgren T, Sato-Mensah R, Petit-Kowalski A
records.abstract: Five hospitals introduced monthly in-situ simulation for medical emergency teams in a random order over 15 months. Across 6,480 real calls, the median time from call to first critical intervention fell by 3.1 minutes after introduction, after adjustment for calendar time. Unplanned intensive care admission within 12 hours of a call did not change (odds ratio 0.96, 95 percent CI 0.81 to 1.14), and death within 24 hours was too rare to compare. Simulations were cancelled in 14 percent of planned months because of staffing. The authors note that five clusters gave imprecise estimates of between-hospital effects.

records.title: Team performance scores in simulation and performance in real rapid response calls: a validation study
records.abstract: We compared the scores of 38 rapid response teams on a standard simulation checklist with blinded ratings of the same teams in video-recorded real calls. Simulation checklist scores correlated weakly with real-call performance (correlation coefficient 0.21). Time to first critical intervention in simulation correlated better with the same time in real calls than checklist scores did. Teams that scored highly in simulation often lost role clarity in crowded real calls. The authors caution against using simulation checklist scores as the main outcome of team training.

records.title: Unannounced in-situ simulation on working wards: safety events, cancellations and staff experience
records.abstract: We reviewed 212 unannounced in-situ simulations run on medical and surgical wards over three years. Three simulations were interrupted by a real call on the same ward and stopped at once, with no delay to the real call. No patient harm was attributed to a simulation. In a staff questionnaire, 41 percent of ward nurses reported anxiety when an unannounced simulation began, and several were unsure at first whether the event was real. Clear signage, a stop word and advance notice to the ward manager were added after the first year.

records.title: Debriefing structure and learning in interprofessional simulation: a systematic review
records.authors: Harcourt-Adeyemi N, Rasmussen-Tanaka B, Oduya-Grieve C
records.abstract: We included 27 studies of debriefing after interprofessional simulation. Structured debriefing with a trained facilitator was associated with better learning outcomes than unstructured discussion in most comparisons, but outcomes were mostly knowledge and self-rated confidence measured immediately after the session. Only four studies measured behaviour in clinical practice, and none measured patient outcomes. Debriefs longer than 20 minutes were no better than shorter ones. Study quality was low to moderate, and most studies were run in simulation centres rather than on clinical wards, so their relevance to in-situ programmes is uncertain.

records.title: Families' experience of rapid response calls on general wards
records.abstract: We spoke with 18 family members who had been present when a rapid response team was called for a relative on a general ward. Families described confusion about who the arriving clinicians were and what their roles were, being asked to leave without explanation, and a lack of information after the team left. Several families had noticed their relative's deterioration before staff did and did not know how to raise concern. Families valued a named person who explained what was happening. Participants came from two hospitals and were contacted by ward managers.

records.title: Latent safety threats identified by in-situ simulation on general wards
records.abstract: Across 146 in-situ simulations on general wards in three hospitals, teams and observers identified a mean of 1.8 latent safety threats per simulation, such as missing airway equipment, wrong suction connectors, blocked bed access and unclear calling procedures. Most threats were fixed within a month. Hospitals that fed threats into a safety tracking system resolved more of them than hospitals that relied on informal follow-up. The study did not measure whether resolving threats changed real-call outcomes, and threats were classified by the simulation faculty without a second rater.

records.title: Intracluster correlation of rapid response outcomes between hospitals: estimates for planning cluster studies
records.abstract: We estimated intracluster correlation coefficients for rapid response call outcomes from 41,300 calls in 22 hospitals over three years. The coefficient was 0.04 for time from call to first critical intervention, 0.02 for unplanned intensive care admission within 12 hours and 0.01 for death within 24 hours. Coefficients were larger for hospitals of very different size and were stable across years. The authors provide the estimates, with their confidence intervals, for sample size calculations in cluster and stepped-wedge studies of rapid response interventions.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. In-situ simulation for rapid response teams was followed by shorter times to the first critical intervention in one uncontrolled study and in a five-hospital stepped evaluation, but unplanned intensive care admission did not change and death was too rare to compare. Simulation checklist scores predict real-call performance poorly, so real-call measures should carry the evaluation. Unannounced simulations can be stopped safely for real calls but cause anxiety among ward staff. Structured debriefing improves immediate learning, and simulations expose latent safety threats. Families describe confusion about the team's roles. Intracluster correlations from 22 hospitals give planning values for a stepped design with few hospitals.
response.gradeRationale: One multi-site stepped evaluation with imprecise estimates, uncontrolled single-site data and indirect evidence on debriefing and measurement; certainty that in-situ simulation shortens time to first critical intervention is low, and very low for patient outcomes.
response.summary: Eight retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims; certainty low.

steps.note: Appraisal of the eight retrieved records (S13); certainty over inspected records (G1).

contexts: rapid response teams of nurse, respiratory therapist and physician
response.reading: The programme acts on teams (role clarity, speed), on wards (latent safety threats, ward nurse escalation) and indirectly on families. Real-call timing responds to training in the retrieved evidence while admissions do not, and simulation checklist scores are poor proxies for real performance. With four hospitals, clustering and calendar time dominate the analysis. The qualitative strand is needed to explain differences between hospitals that four clusters cannot estimate.

response.finer: Feasible within the grant and faculty time; interesting to education leads and the health authority; novel in combining real-call outcomes with experience across hospitals; ethical with safety rules and consent; relevant to case review findings.
response.summary: One quantitative and one qualitative question.

response.rationale: The quantitative question (does real-call timing improve) and the qualitative question (how and why, and why hospitals differ) need both strands. A stepped introduction across four hospitals in random order lets each hospital serve as its own control while adjusting for calendar time (c1), with planning values from the intracluster correlations (c4). Real-call outcomes carry the evaluation because checklist scores are poor proxies (c2). Safety rules for unannounced simulation follow the retrieved experience (c3), and latent threats are tracked (c5).

response.overview: Stepped multi-site mixed methods evaluation over 18 months in four hospitals: a three-month baseline in all hospitals, then monthly in-situ simulation with structured debriefing introduced one hospital every three months in a random order, with a quantitative strand on real calls and a qualitative strand on experience, integrated by joint displays.
response.population: All rapid response calls at the four hospitals, about 2,860 a year; rapid response team members, ward nurses and families for the qualitative strand.
response.exposure: Monthly unannounced in-situ simulation on a general ward with the on-duty rapid response team, followed by a 20-minute structured debrief by trained faculty; latent safety threats logged in the hospital safety tracking system.
response.procedures: Call data (activation time, first critical intervention time, disposition) are abstracted from the rapid response call record by trained abstractors blind to the programme phase where possible. Simulations follow a safety protocol: advance notice to the ward manager, signage, a stop word, and immediate cancellation if a real call occurs. The qualitative strand interviews team members, ward nurses and families and observes debriefs in each hospital after introduction.

response.designSummary: Stepped design with four hospitals and six three-month periods (one baseline period in all hospitals, then one hospital introduced every three months in a random order), restricted to adult ward calls; linear mixed model for time to first critical intervention with period and phase as fixed effects.
response.sampleSize: About 2,310 adult ward calls a year give about 145 calls per hospital per three-month period, or about 3,470 calls over 18 months. With a standard deviation of 6 minutes and an intracluster correlation of 0.04 (claim c4), the stepped design with four hospitals and six periods has roughly 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect a 2-minute reduction, which is smaller than the 3.1-minute fall seen in the five-hospital evaluation. Because four clusters give few degrees of freedom, the analysis uses a small-sample correction and the result is reported as an estimate with its interval, not a verdict. Unplanned intensive care admission (intracluster correlation 0.02, about 12 percent of calls) is underpowered for an effect of the size seen elsewhere and is reported descriptively with its interval.
response.primaryAnalysis: Linear mixed model for log-transformed time to first critical intervention with fixed effects for period (calendar time) and programme phase, a random effect for hospital and a hospital-by-period random effect, Kenward-Roger small-sample correction; the phase effect is back-transformed to a ratio of median times with its 95 percent confidence interval.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Logistic mixed model for unplanned intensive care admission within 12 hours with the same structure; descriptive counts of deaths within 24 hours by phase; run charts of simulations delivered and latent safety threats resolved; framework analysis of interviews and debrief observations, integrated with the quantitative results in a joint display by hospital.
response.missingData: Calls with a missing first-intervention time are counted by hospital and phase; if more than 5 percent are missing, multiple imputation by chained equations with 20 imputations under a missing-at-random assumption, with a complete-case sensitivity analysis.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary and balancing outcomes are reported with intervals and are not tested for significance.
response.software: R with lme4 and pbkrtest for the quantitative strand; NVivo for the qualitative strand.
overfittingGuards: Model structure and adjustment variables fixed before data collection
No subgroup analysis by hospital beyond the joint display
Checklist scores from simulations kept as a secondary description (claim c2)
response.summary: About 145 adult ward calls per hospital per period give roughly 80 percent power for a 2-minute reduction with a small-sample correction.

steps.note: A fresh Stats reply requested after the edit and the reconciled protocol: applied, and its sample size follows the adult ward population (about 2,310 calls a year), closing the dependency between protocol and stats.

response.risks: Unannounced simulations on working wards could distract staff from real patients, cause anxiety or be mistaken for real emergencies; interviews may touch on distressing calls.
response.consent: Rapid response team members and ward managers consent to the programme in advance and may opt out of being observed; ward nurses are told a simulation may occur on their ward in a given week; manikins are used, never patients; interviews need written consent; families are approached after the patient has stabilised, with interpreters.
response.data: Call records are abstracted with study codes; recordings of debriefs are made only with the team's consent and deleted after transcription.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients and families with limited English, patients on wards with fewer staff at night and patients in the smaller hospitals may benefit least. Scenarios include night-time and interpreter elements, results are reported by hospital size and time of day, and families with limited English are included in interviews with interpreters.
response.effectiveness: Success is a shorter time to first critical intervention with no harm from simulations and an explanation of hospital differences.
response.efficiency: Eight faculty hours a month per hospital and a grant of 48,000.
response.costs: About 21,000 for abstraction, 12,000 for transcription and interpreters, and 15,000 for faculty backfill.
response.grants: Grant SEF-2026-14; a larger authority-wide programme could seek provincial education funding.
response.partnerships: Education leads at the four hospitals, simulation faculty, rapid response teams, ward managers and a family partner from the patient and family advisory council.
response.rebPath: Application to the health authority research ethics board as board of record for the multi-site study; the decision is unknown and no simulation for research purposes or data abstraction begins before approval. Stop rules for real calls are part of the application.
response.limitations: Four hospitals; open programme delivery; call record timing may be imprecise.
response.summary: Safety rules and consent for unannounced simulation, equity reporting and a board of record decision still unknown.

response.partnershipPlan: A family partner and two rapid response team members review the interview guides; ward managers from each hospital review the safety protocol for unannounced simulation.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; anonymised staff comments from last year's case reviews are themed.

response.title: In-situ simulation for rapid response teams in four hospitals: a stepped multi-site mixed methods evaluation
response.abstract: Objective: to evaluate monthly in-situ simulation for rapid response teams on real-call performance and to explain how teams, ward nurses and families experience it. Design: stepped introduction across four hospitals in random order over 18 months with a qualitative strand. Primary outcome: time from call to first critical intervention in adult ward calls. Results and conclusions will be written after the study.
response.introduction: In-situ simulation has shortened time to first critical intervention in a multi-site evaluation, but patient outcomes did not change and simulation scores are poor proxies for real calls.
response.methods: Six three-month periods; hospitals introduced in random order; linear mixed model with period and phase and a small-sample correction; about 3,470 adult ward calls; interviews and debrief observation analysed with the framework method and integrated in joint displays.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present calls by period and hospital, the primary estimate with its interval, secondary and balancing outcomes, delivery and latent safety threats, themes and the joint display.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret the primary estimate given four clusters, use the qualitative strand to explain differences between hospitals, and state implications for the authority's programme.
response.limitations: Four clusters; open delivery; call record timing; the qualitative sample may favour engaged staff.
response.conclusion: To be written after the study; it will not claim effects on patient outcomes that the design cannot detect.
response.reportingChecklist: CONSORT extension for stepped-wedge trials for the quantitative strand, with GRAMMS for the mixed methods report
response.summary: Draft structured for a stepped multi-site mixed methods report with results left empty.
